name: Flour + Water
note: House-made pasta is the star. The agnolotti and the tajarin are life-changing. Neapolitan-style pizzas from the wood-fired oven are equally impressive. Reservations essential at this pasta temple.

name: House of Prime Rib

plato.es: prime rib cortado en la mesa

note: Old-school SF since 1949. Prime rib carved tableside from silver carts, Yorkshire pudding, and creamed spinach. The martinis are perfect. A time capsule of classic American dining.
address: 1906 Van Ness Ave, San Francisco, CA 94109

name: Ju-ni
note: Intimate 12-seat omakase sushi bar from former Saison chef Geoffrey Lee. The $300+ tasting menu features pristine fish flown in from Tsukiji Market. Watching the chef's knife work up close is part of the experience. Reservations essential.

name: Lazy Bear

plato.en: a tasting menu and that bread and butter
plato.es: menú de degustación y ese pan con mantequilla

note: One of my most memorable fine-dining experiences in San Francisco. The cultured butter and bread were exceptional, but what made the meal truly special was the original shared-table dinner-party format, with everyone eating together. Lazy Bear no longer seats guests communally, but the nostalgic, hyper-seasonal tasting menu and that incredible bread and butter still make it a recommendation.

name: Mijoté

plato.es: el menú francés de la semana

note: Modern French bistro with a California soul. The duck confit and the bone marrow with escargot are standouts. Natural wine program is exceptional. Intimate space perfect for special occasions.

review.shareTitle: Mijoté: The sushi bar where you get a French omakase in the Mission
personal: I didn't really understand why I liked this restaurant so much the first time I was there, but it was probably because I was sitting at the bar next to the chef and he was finishing all these delicious French plates in front of me. And then it hit me. This used to be a sushi bar, and they kept that dynamic. They bring all the experience of cooking French food in Paris into San Francisco, but they do it and serve the plates with all the finishing touches right in front of you. That's kind of nice. Mijoté has a great, minimalistic, fixed-price menu with a couple of add-ons. You're going to love their bread and check the pairings or just see what's eclectic today in their wine list because they always have some great stuff. And make sure to ask to be seated at the bar. That's the best location.

The menu and service are unpretentious and you get very good French food.

name: Mister Jiu's
note: Try the duck. This is a Michelin-starred Chinese American restaurant in Chinatown -the original Chinatown of San Francisco. The video will show you how much care they put into that duck, and they also do amazing hot pot and cocktails.

review.shareTitle: Mister Jiu's: always go for the Liberty duck
personal: Mister Jiu's: always go for the Liberty duck.
I really like to eat duck in Chinese restaurants. Duck and rice. Maybe a soup by the side. It does not have to be fancy. When you want the best in town, head to Mister Jiu's.
Beautiful bar upstairs: Moongate Lounge. Great cocktails, beautiful decor. They also do fancy events if you get invited.

Talk about the duck. Liberty Farms, Sonoma. Pre-order it with the reservation. The treatment that makes the skin crispier. I have had my fair share of this dish, and I am still impressed by the flavor, the texture, and the crunch. The condiments. The little tortillas. Somebody will say those are not tortillas. If you were raised with them, you see them anywhere. Mix duck, condiments, veggies. Enjoy.
Now it is a $125 Peking duck banquet you can pre-order. The à la carte duck sells out. Pre-order it with the reservation.
Definitely the best restaurant in Chinatown. Sorry China Live. You are trendy and I love you too. El señor Jiu and I have some good stories.
Reserve in advance. Pre-order the duck. I repeat, go for the duck.

faqs.question: Do I need to pre-order the duck at Mister Jiu's?

Menlo Park and Mint Plaza get special mention. Sister properties: Kayah by Burma Love at Chase Center, and Teakwood by Burma Love in Hayes Valley.

review.shareTitle: Burma Love: the Valencia branch is the best one, get the tea leaf salad.
personal: The Valencia branch is the best one. Find an excuse to reserve the big round table: bring a group so you can try it all. Get there early for a drink at the bar.

You have to try the tea leaf salad because those fermented tea leaves are amazing and it has a great umami magic. Also, the coconut rice is great and I always include at least a curry, a soup with noodles, and some chicken.
Menlo Park and Mint Plaza get special mention. Same family, same tea leaf salad, a different room: Springline on the Peninsula, and the downtown dining room on Mint Plaza.

Now there are sister properties too. Kayah by Burma Love is at Thrive City next to Chase Center, the one you want before a Warriors game. Teakwood by Burma Love is the Hayes Valley room, more of a fire-warmed, special-occasion table.
This place introduced Burmese cuisine to many Americans, and Valencia is still the one I trust with a whole afternoon.

note: El Chato is that Spanish corner that brings vibes of Madrid to the Mission. Natural wine bar with great owners. Go for the tapas, the tortilla española, navajas, jamón and cheese, and ask for chatos. Trust the wine stand. On a sunny day, hang out outside.

review.shareTitle: El Chato is that Spanish corner that brings vibes of Madrid to the Mission.
personal: This corner really makes Madrid a thing in the Mission. Beautiful place, great owners, and the kind of bar you end up trusting with a whole afternoon.

Spending a lot of time in Madrid, Barcelona, Granada and San Sebastián, you develop a love for the passion of Spanish food. And finding that same character in their owners, that love for making a tortilla taste good and caring for the bread and the vermuts, that's what makes El Chato a place where you feel in España.

It's a natural wine bar. Go for the tapas, the tortilla española, and the wines. They're just amazing. I really enjoy the navajas, and their jamón and cheese selection. Ask for some chatos so you can try more of what they have on the menu. The owners' passion shows in the food and in a list that leans on small European producers. The tortilla is simple, soft inside and golden at the edges.

They serve that tortilla as a pintxo on grilled bread with piquillo and allioli. Get pan con tomate with it, and spread the tomato yourself. The toasted jamón sandwich with melted cheese and piparras is the other plate I keep in the middle of the table.

During the World Cup this was a great community for following Spain. Locals and Spaniards hanging out, sharing an Estrella, calling the goals, passing around tortilla de patata and their vermut. They have a great non-alcoholic one for those early matches. The team is friendly. Trust their recommendations from the wine stand.

On a sunny day (the Mission gets better weather than the rest of the city) you can hang out outside. That corner doesn't just feel Mission. A friend said it could be Roma in Mexico City, Castellana in Madrid, Palermo Soho in Buenos Aires, or Providencia in Chile. There's a vibe in the corner.
Feels like a slice of Madrid in the Mission, with warm hospitality and flavors that actually hold up.

personal: This is my top burrito in San Francisco. Since appearing in the Michelin guide, the line got really big. Still worth it. No rice, pure love of carne asada. Funny that you get a burrito at La Taqueria. Go for the carne asada, make it supreme, ask for extra guac if you want. The carne asada is grilled to order.

If you are repeating, make sure to try the variety of tacos. The salsa is amazing. They even have issues with people stealing the containers. Part of the Mission's taqueria culture for decades, La Taqueria has been doing this long enough that the name is a little joke on first-timers: you come for the burrito, then you come back for the tacos.
We are still missing a proper burrito photo. For now, at least we have the carne asada on the grill and the actual tacos on the table.

review.shareTitle: Plow, the definite place for brunch in San Francisco
personal: Plow, the definite place for brunch in San Francisco.

Every time somebody asks me where to go for brunch, I mention Plow. I really like the place. It’s a great destination on Potrero Hill, and you’ll always find a line on a busy day. Go on a Wednesday, or get there early, and you can get in. It’s definitely worth it. Behind the bar, happy cooks are always surprising you with breakfasts: eggs, bread, and sometimes a Chinese version of breakfast. It’s always a fantastic experience. The coffee, the ambience, and the flavors. Try the different menus and see what you like.

Plow’s great. It’s worth the wait. If the line is really hard, still put your name on the list, walk to Farley’s (1315 18th St) half a block away, grab a tea or a coffee, and come back. I’ve had some of the best conversations in that line. If you’re lucky, you’re just getting in. I still remember during the pandemic they kept serving breakfast. I’m not sure about delivery, but I remember picking up directly. They always handed over those packages with a great smile and a lot of thanks. Plow is where you go for breakfast and really enjoy it. That’s why San Francisco has spots that are worth it. This is my best example.
Try to avoid weekends. It’s super crowded. Get there early on a weekday and you’ll have the best experience.

faqs.question: What should I order at Plow?
faqs.answer: Eggs, bread, whatever they are surprising you with behind the bar. Sometimes a Chinese version of breakfast. Try the different menus and see what you like.

review.reservationTip: No reservations. Stick to weekdays; get there early. If the line is hard, put your name down and walk to Farley's (1315 18th St) for coffee.

name: Reem's California Mission
note: Arab street food meets California ingredients. Their mana'eesh (flatbreads) are baked to order in a custom oven. The za'atar with cheese and the lamb flatbread are exceptional. Owner Reem Assil creates food that tells stories of Arab heritage.

name: San Ho Won
note: Chef Corey Lee and Jeong-In Hwang's Michelin-starred Korean charcoal barbecue restaurant. The house menu is generous, the banchan and vegetables are as carefully handled as the meat, and the charcoal-grilled beef is the centerpiece. Reservations can be difficult, so book when they are released.

review.shareTitle: San Ho Won, the michelin star korean bbq in San Francisco.
personal: If you love Korean BBQ, this is the fancy version in San Francisco. You will be full, you will be happy, and you can get leftover food to go. I always enjoy going with friends to a Korean barbecue, but for an upscale experience, San Ho Won is the one you're looking for if you want to impress. Not only will they make great barbecue meat for you, but their selection of beverages and add-ons is superb. If you've ever gone to a Korean barbecue and were worried about overcooking the meat or not having it at the right point, that's what San Ho Won will do for you.

Reservations are hard to get in advance unless you want to try the last serving at night, and that late seating might be a heavy meal. Still, San Ho Won is a very good deal: a Michelin-star menu, a very good selection of meat, and a reservation that is worth sharing with a group of four or even six people. Plan ahead, and sometimes check for the very last options in the schedule because they tend to open up occasionally. This is definitely a place worth visiting in San Francisco.
We did a small reel when we visited. It is a better way to appreciate the tasting menu. Check it out.

faqs.question: Is San Ho Won walk-in friendly?
faqs.answer: Walk-ins are a long shot. Reservations are hard to get in advance unless you want the last serving at night, and that late seating can be a heavy meal. Book on Resy when you can, and keep an eye on last-minute openings.

faqs.question: Is San Ho Won worth it for a group?
faqs.answer: Yes. It is a very good deal for a Michelin-star menu: a strong selection of meat, leftovers to take home, and a reservation that is worth sharing with four or even six people. You will be full and you will be happy.

faqs.question: What makes San Ho Won special?
faqs.answer: If you love Korean BBQ, this is the fancy version in San Francisco. The staff grill the meat for you at the table, so you are not worrying about overcooking it, and the portions are generous enough that leftover food to go is part of the night.

guest.author: Friends
guest.intro: Remarks from other friends I enjoyed this experience with:
paragraphs: In San Ho Won the short rib was amazing. All in general was very good. It’s a different experience for Korean BBQ. Feels upper middle class while usually a BBQ experience is more a popular meal.

name: Starbelly

plato.en: fried chicken sandwich on the patio
plato.es: sándwich de pollo frito en el patio

note: California comfort food with a great back patio. Their fried chicken sandwich and pizzas are neighborhood favorites. Excellent brunch spot with bottomless mimosas. Dog-friendly patio.

name: The Mill

plato.en: thick toast and Four Barrel coffee
plato.es: tostada gruesa y café Four Barrel

note: Famous for thick-cut toast topped with seasonal ingredients and Four Barrel coffee. The $4 toast became a symbol of SF's artisanal food movement. Their bread from Josey Baker Bread is exceptional, and the almond butter toast with sea salt is iconic.

name: Tony's Pizza Napoletana

plato.en: a Margherita from the 73 a day
plato.es: una de las 73 Margheritas del día

note: It's a place in San Francisco that has some awards, especially if you want to go for the Margherita or the Mozzarella one. They have seven different ovens for different styles, and they say that some of the pizzas will be sold out. I've never seen any pizza sold out, but just go early. Make the line. It's totally worth it.

review.shareTitle: Tony's Pizza Napoletana: Margherita in North Beach, Golden Boy if you just want a slice
personal: Glad this is one of the best pizzas in America. Glad it exists in North Beach and makes San Francisco special. When I tried pizza in Napoli, I was confused, hehehe.

That said: good pizza, expensive pizza. Really good pizza. Try the specials. They only make 73 Margheritas a day. You usually get one if you care. Order a Margherita if you are in the room. I remember you cannot get that one to go. Only get pizza to go if you are walking to Washington Square and want to skip the line.
No reservations. Crowded. For sharing good pizza with friends, this is the place. Just a snack: walk a block to Golden Boy Pizza. Square slices. Really good.
In a city that will never match New York on pizza, this is our institution. Big, pricey, worth it.

name: Wise Sons Jewish Delicatessen
note: Modern Jewish deli serving pastrami on rye that rivals NYC's best, plus bagels, lox, and babka. Their challah French toast at brunch is exceptional. A taste of the Lower East Side in the Mission, with multiple locations across the city.

name: Z & Y
note: Explosive Sichuan flavors, the tea-smoked duck and mapo tofu will test your spice tolerance. Their 'Explosive Chili Chicken' is buried in chilies. One of the best regional Chinese restaurants in America.

name: Balompié Café
note: Authentic pupuseria serving handmade pupusas stuffed with cheese, beans, chicharrón, or loroco. Watch them made fresh through the window. Their curtido (pickled cabbage) and salsa roja are perfect accompaniments. Cash only, incredibly affordable.

review.shareTitle: Balompié Café: legit pupusas, and the bill comes in a soccer shoe
personal: I really love how the bill comes in a small soccer shoe at the end. The pupusas are legit. I have been a couple of times with people from El Salvador who really miss them. San Francisco has a lot of amazing places, and this is one of my best options. I miss pupusas too, since they are very common in Guatemala.
This is not a place to discuss tech or bring your techie friends. This is a place to enjoy Salvadoran food.

My take: the pupusa de queso with loroco. If you don't know what loroco is, it's the Salvadoran vegetable, as English menus call it: actually the edible flower bud of a vine (Fernaldia pandurata) grown in El Salvador and Guatemala, with a green, herbal flavor, a bit like asparagus or squash blossom, that melts into the cheese. You have to try it. The best version is just with cheese, loroco con queso. They also do some exotic combinations (like Panchita's, another good place, does), but I stick with the classics. The other good combination is the Mixta, the one with chicharrón and also beans. That's a very nice mix, but not everyone likes the beans, so be cautious with that. Central Americans, we really love it. Better to order pupusas and not the combos, but I understand why they push the combos for people who don't have the habit of eating pupusas.

And I really believe you need to eat this with your hands, so just go to the bathroom, wash your hands, and then enjoy your pupusas. Put the curtido on the side of the pupusa first, then some of the salsa on top of it, and mix it. The best thing is when you grab a piece of pupusa, curtido, and salsa with your hand and eat it. That's how it really makes sense, and that's how you will enjoy pupusas as a real salvadoreño: with a Kolashampan, the orange Salvadoran soda. Really, really good. Or a beer, if it's noon and they're watching some soccer on the screens.
You will definitely hear the Salvadoran accent and understand how legit this place is.

name: Bi-Rite Creamery
note: San Francisco's most beloved ice cream shop. The salted caramel is legendary, and seasonal flavors like honey lavender showcase local ingredients. Expect long lines on sunny days - it's a Mission District ritual. Their soft serve with olive oil and sea salt is a must-try.

name: Farley's
note: Potrero Hill's community living room since 1989. Great coffee, fresh pastries, and a mix of locals working on laptops and families grabbing breakfast. Their outdoor seating on 18th Street is perfect for people watching. A true neighborhood institution.

name: Four Barrel Coffee
note: Valencia Street's coffee temple with a massive roasting facility visible from the cafe. Single-origin pour-overs and expertly pulled espresso. The industrial-chic space with high ceilings and communal seating embodies Mission District coffee culture.

name: Kingdom of Dumplings
note: No-frills spot for authentic Beijing-style dumplings. Their lamb & cumin dumplings and the hand-pulled biang biang noodles are exceptional. Cash only, worth the trek to the Richmond.

igPosts.text: Kingdom of Dumplings and Moku Yakitori-Ya

name: Mosto

plato.en: tacos al pastor off the trompo

note: Their tacos al pastor are amazing because they have a proper trompo, and they also have a great mezcal selection. Unfortunately, lately they are also building burgers, and despite the fact that they are trendy, I think that they are losing part of the essence that made me recommend them at the first time.

review.shareTitle: Mosto: The mezcal bar of the Mission where you can have good pastor tacos.
personal: We have a real mezcal bar in San Francisco. Is the sister little property of Tacolicious. Mosto/El Burger also has good pastor. Skip the burgers.

There's a picture of Obama, and that guy knew about good food when I saw him on a little banquito in Hanoi eating bún chả with Bourdain, so I will trust his selection of tacos. Not sure if he paired them with some mezcal.

The tacos al pastor come from a proper trompo and remain the reason to go. Carved with char, pineapple, and salsa. We did a small reel when we visited. Check it out. They have a good mezcal selection too. Lately they are also making burgers, but I think that loses part of what made me recommend them the first time. Stick to the pastor. Skip the burgers.

faqs.question: Is Mosto the bar next to Tacolicious?
faqs.answer: Tacolicious has a small bar next door. Might be the extra space but for me, it has always been the main attraction. A full mezcal bar, with pastor tacos. Intimate. With banda linda. The pastor that the Mission gives.

faqs.answer: Stick to the pastor. It comes from a proper trompo, carved with char, pineapple, and salsa. Skip the burgers. That loses part of what made me recommend them.

faqs.question: Do they have mezcal?
faqs.answer: Yes. Good mezcal selection. That is half the point.

name: Noe Cafe

plato.en: the breakfast sandwich in the parklet
plato.es: el breakfast sandwich en el parklet

note: Known for perfectly prepared chai lattes and their avocado toast topped with hemp seeds and chili flakes. A neighborhood gem that embodies Noe Valley's village-like charm.
address: 1299 Sanchez St (at 26th St), San Francisco, CA 94114

review.shareTitle: Noe Cafe, my go-to for a meeting and an easy coffee in Noe Valley
personal: It's a really cool coffee shop in Noe Valley, on the Sanchez Slow Street, very child and dog friendly.

I love it. They have two branches, the other one in Mission Bay, but the one I really like is Noe Cafe in Noe Valley. They have a nice parklet, so you can really grab your coffee outside. They also have some inside tables that aren't always available, but the vibe is pretty good.

Occasionally during the week they bring a guy who sells tacos, wearing a big taco hat. It's the place where you hang out when you live in the Noe Valley area, but it's also visited by a lot of tech people and VCs.

I really recommend their sandwiches and their toast. The avocado toast is really good, and I usually get the breakfast sandwich. Other than the different coffees, they also have a selection of kombuchas, and they have a liquor license, so if you go a little later in the day you can also grab a beer. It's a great spot for a beer, and whenever there are festivities on Sanchez, the community and the ambience are really good.
Some other friends always say it's a very chill place and a great place for meetings, and I agree. It's my go-to place to have a meeting, or just to enjoy an easy coffee in Noe Valley.
Noe Cafe, the best place to have a coffee, chill and hang out with your friends in Noe Valley.

faqs.question: Where is Noe Cafe?
faqs.answer: 1299 Sanchez St at 26th St, Noe Valley, on the Sanchez Slow Street. There's a parklet outside and some tables inside.

faqs.question: What should I order at Noe Cafe?
faqs.answer: I usually get the Breakfast Sandwich. The avocado toast is really good too. Besides coffee, they have kombuchas, and beer later in the day.

faqs.question: What are Noe Cafe's hours?
faqs.answer: Mon–Wed 7am–5pm, Thu–Sun 7am–6pm.

name: Shoji
note: Their signature matcha soft serve and expertly prepared pour-over coffee make this a must-visit. The minimalist Japanese aesthetic creates a zen moment in busy SOMA.
address: 140 New Montgomery St, Suite 1, San Francisco, CA 94105

name: Swan Oyster Depot
note: I recently made the line and it was totally worth it. Not only do they have amazing oysters, but always ask for a sample, but also their sashimi plates are great, as well as the clam chowder soup. Really recommend it. Worth the wait. Remember that it's cash only and get a beer.

review.shareTitle: Swan Oyster Depot: Sicilian sashimi on Polk
personal: I was lucky that I didn't have to wait this day, but usually, you actually have to wait a while to get there. The seafood is fresh, good quality, and if you happen to ask for a crab cocktail or the sashimi, you're definitely going to have a feast.
Great beer, great people, and a packed line to get what you need. So, happily to recommend this, and as good as it gets when you want some seafood.

dishes.description: The famous plate. Fresh is the point.

dishes.name: Crab cocktail
dishes.description: Ask for a crab cocktail if you want a feast.

faqs.question: Does Swan Oyster Depot take reservations?
faqs.answer: No. First come, first served. Usually you wait a while. I was lucky one day and did not have to. Arrive early if you can.

faqs.question: What should I order at Swan Oyster Depot?
faqs.answer: Ask for a crab cocktail or the sashimi and you are going to have a feast. Fresh seafood, good quality. Great beer too.

faqs.question: Is Swan Oyster Depot worth the wait?
faqs.answer: Yes. Opened in 1912, so about 114 years. Great beer, great people, packed line. As good as it gets when you want seafood.

review.reservationTip: No reservations -arrive before 11am to beat the line
review.idealFor: Seafood lovers seeking an authentic SF experience

name: Trad Bone Broth
note: Takeout-only bone broth cafe on 24th Street: broths on tap (beef, chicken, a Korean-style Seoul Broth, and a vegetarian option) plus made-to-order savory and sweet broth drinks. Open Tue-Sun 9am-7pm, closed Mondays.

name: Yuanbao Jiaozi
note: Handmade dumplings are the star. Try the pork & chive and the fish dumplings. Their hand-pulled noodles in rich broths are equally exceptional. A neighborhood favorite for authentic Northern Chinese cuisine.

name: Zuni Café
note: Their legendary roast chicken for two with bread salad is a San Francisco institution, order it and wait the 45 minutes, it's worth it. This James Beard Award-winning restaurant has been defining California cuisine since 1979. Also try their Caesar salad and oysters.

name: Arsicault Bakery
note: Home of SF's best croissant - buttery, flaky perfection that regularly wins 'Best Croissant' awards. Their almond croissant and kouign-amann are equally exceptional. Arrive early, they sell out fast.

name: Tartine Bakery
note: Home to the city's most famous morning buns and country bread that launched a thousand sourdough obsessions. Their croissants are equally legendary. This bakery transformed American bread culture and remains a pilgrimage site for bakers worldwide.
